title: How the Web Works
summary: When you open a URL the browser resolves DNS, opens a TCP+TLS connection, sends an **HTTP request**, and renders the **response** — fetching CSS/JS/images as it parses. Almost every performance, caching, and CORS problem is really a networking problem.

subtopics.title: DNS resolution
subtopics.explanation: The human-readable domain is looked up and resolved to an IP address before any request is sent; results are cached at several layers.

subtopics.title: TCP + TLS handshake
subtopics.explanation: A connection is established (TCP), and for HTTPS a TLS handshake negotiates encryption. These round-trips cost time before the first byte.

subtopics.title: The request/response
subtopics.explanation: The client sends an HTTP request (method, path, headers); the server returns a status, headers, and a body (often HTML).

subtopics.title: Progressive rendering
subtopics.explanation: The browser parses HTML as it streams, discovers subresources, and fetches them in parallel; render-blocking CSS/JS gate first paint.

foundations.overview: When you open a URL, your browser resolves the domain to an IP via DNS, opens a connection (TCP, plus TLS for HTTPS), sends an HTTP request, and the server responds with HTML; the browser then fetches linked CSS/JS/images and renders the page. Understanding this round-trip explains latency, caching, and where things break.
foundations.formalDefinition: The web is a client-server system over HTTP: a client (browser) sends requests to a server identified by a URL (resolved via DNS), and the server returns responses; assets are delivered over one or more connections and rendered by the browser.
foundations.whyItMatters: Nearly every frontend performance, caching, CORS, and debugging problem is a networking problem underneath. You can't reason about load time or a failed request without the request/response mental model.
foundations.mentalModel: Ordering at a restaurant: DNS is finding the address, the request is your order, the server is the kitchen, the response is the food, and a CDN is a nearby branch that keeps popular dishes ready.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser parses HTML as it streams, discovers subresources, and fetches them (often multiplexed over HTTP/2); render-blocking CSS and synchronous JS delay first paint.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Diagnosing a slow page (DNS/TLS/TTFB vs download vs render), understanding why an API call fails with CORS, and knowing what a CDN caches at the edge.
foundations.businessImpact: Latency directly affects conversion and bounce; the round-trip model is the basis of every performance win.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Lets you read the Network panel, reason about caching/CDNs, and debug failures at the correct layer instead of guessing.
foundations.performanceImpact: Each phase — DNS, TCP/TLS, TTFB, download, render — is a place to save time; HTTP/2 multiplexing and caching remove round-trips.

commonMisconceptions.reality: Latency, HTTPS, CORS, caching, and compression all differ — many bugs only appear in production.

commonMisconceptions.myth: The browser downloads everything, then renders.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It streams and renders progressively, fetching subresources as it parses the HTML.

theory.question: Walk me through what happens when you type a URL and press Enter.
theory.directAnswer: The browser resolves the domain to an IP via DNS, opens a TCP connection (and a TLS handshake for HTTPS), then sends an HTTP GET request. The server responds with HTML; the browser parses it, discovers CSS/JS/images and fetches them (render-blocking resources gate first paint), builds the DOM and CSSOM, then lays out, paints, and composites the page. A CDN may serve cacheable assets from the edge.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The full client-server round-trip from URL to rendered pixels.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: It's the canonical systems question because it touches DNS, transport, HTTP, caching, and rendering at once.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: DNS -> TCP/TLS -> HTTP request -> response -> subresource fetches -> parse/render pipeline.

theory.whyImportant: It reveals whether you understand the layers between a click and a painted page.

nestedTopics.title: Where caching helps
nestedTopics.explanation: DNS cache, HTTP caching, and the CDN each remove work from the critical path.

followUps.question: Where would you look first if the page is slow?
followUps.answer: The Network panel: split DNS/TLS/TTFB (server/network) from download and render (client) to attack the dominant cost.

keyTakeaways: A page load is DNS -> TCP/TLS -> HTTP request -> response -> fetch subresources -> render.
HTTPS adds a TLS handshake; HTTP/2 multiplexes many requests over one connection.
Most 'frontend' performance and CORS bugs are networking problems.
A CDN serves cacheable assets from an edge near the user.
